events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
Endeavour Group Limited (Endeavour Group) proposes to acquire a
leasehold interest for retail space in a new development at 1 & 3
Careel Head Road, Avalon NSW 2107 (the Proposed Site) from
Avalon DM Pty Ltd (the Lessor) (the Acquisition).
Endeavour Group intends to operate a Dan Murphy's liquor store on
the Proposed Site, with a trading area of approximately 340 square
metres.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Endeavour, is an Australian public company that
primarily operates:
▪ retail liquor stores nationwide under the BWS and Dan
Murphy’s brands;
▪ licensed hotel venues under the ALH Hotels banner in all
states and territories. These venues are individually branded
venues offering on-premises food and drinks, entertainment,
gaming services and, in some cases, accommodation; and
▪ Pinnacle Drinks, a manufacturer and distributor of liquor
products, which it distributes exclusively to the Endeavour
retail and hotel network in Australia
The Lessor is an independent, Australian privately-owned special
purpose vehicle established for the purposes of the acquisition and
development of the property.

determination_table_content.item:
Overlap and relationship
between the parties
determination_table_content.details:
The leasehold interest would be an input into Endeavour Group’s
existing takeaway packaged liquor operations.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form. The ACCC also considered feedback from third
parties which raised concerns that the Acquisition would result in
existing competitors exiting the market.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
▪ The proposed Dan Murphy’s would face competition from
multiple alternative suppliers in the surrounding area.
▪ The likely degree of overlap between the Proposed Site and
existing Endeavour Group stores is not significant in the
context of the local area. The closest existing Endeavour
Group sites to the Proposed Site are BWS Newport (3.9 km
away) and Dan Murphy’s Mona Vale (6.7 km away).
▪ The aggregation arising from the Acquisition, including
considering previous acquisitions by Endeavour Group in the
last three years, is not sufficient to meaningfully change
competition over a relevant broader market.
The ACCC notes that some third parties raised concerns about a
liquor licence being granted for the Proposed Site, and the suitability
of the Proposed Site for liquor retailing. However, these concerns did
not relate to the likely competitive effects of the Acquisition and
were therefore outside the scope of the ACCC’s assessment.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

The acquirer, Accenture, is a global professional services company
headquartered in Dublin, Ireland. It provides a broad range of
services across strategy, consulting, digital, technology, and
operations designed to assist public and private clients by bringing
client-specific industry solutions and services to accelerate

marketing, sales, service, commerce, design, digital products, data

The target, Whalar Agency, is a global creator and social media tech-
enabled service business with proprietary platforms carved out from
the Whalar Group.
Whalar Agency comprises the Whalar Group’s creator and influencer
marketing services agency that designs, executes and measures
end-to-end influencer marketing campaigns for enterprise brands,
supported by proprietary AI-enabled technology.
The parties both supply marketing and communications services in
Australia, including digital advertising and creator/influencer
advertising services.

In making this notification waiver determination, the Australian
Competition and Consumer Commission (the ACCC) has considered
the information provided with the notification waiver application and
had regard to the factors in section 51ABV(2)(b) of the Competition

a. the parties’ combined share in the supply of digital
advertising services and the supply of creator/influencer
advertising services in Australia is low and the increase in

b. there are alternative suppliers of digital advertising services

c. there appears to be a low risk of foreclosure or other anti-
competitive vertical effects resulting from exclusionary
conduct post-acquisition.
In these circumstances, the ACCC does not consider it necessary to
reach a concluded view on the likelihood of the notification
thresholds being met.

determination_table_content.details:
Telstra International Networks Pty Ltd (TINS) and Telstra Australia
Networks Pty Ltd (TANS), each a wholly owned subsidiary of Telstra
Group Limited (Telstra), applied for a notification waiver in respect
of their proposed acquisition of indefeasible rights of use (IRUs) over
dark fibre on three new subsea cables (the Tabua, Proa and Bulikula
cables, together, the Pacific Connect Cables) from Manta Ray
Solutions LLC and Perch Infrastructure Pty Ltd, being indirect
subsidiaries of Google LLC, as described in the transaction
documents provided as part of the application (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABV(1)(a) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition is not required to be
notified.
13 July 2026

TINS and TANS, supply international telecommunications services to
government, enterprise, and business customers outside Australia.
In Australia, Telstra provides mobile, fixed-line, internet, and data
services to consumers, businesses, and government, amongst other
telecommunications and technology infrastructure.
Manta Ray Solutions LLC and Perch Infrastructure Pty Ltd, are
indirect subsidiaries of Google LLC, a Delaware limited liability
company owned by Alphabet, Inc.
The IRUs to be acquired will provide Telstra with an exclusive right to
use certain fibre pairs on the Pacific Connect Cables for a period of
15 years. Telstra will have the ability to sell some or all of the
capacity that it activates on these cables to third parties.
The subsea dark fibre being acquired by Telstra will need to be ‘lit’ by
Telstra to enable live services. Telstra will need to install its own
electronic equipment, known as submarine line termination
equipment, to activate capacity on each of its designated fibre pairs.

In making this notification waiver determination, the Australian
Competition and Consumer Commission (the ACCC) has considered
the information provided with the notification waiver application, and
had regard to the factors in section 51ABV(2)(b) of the Competition
and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act).
Based on the information currently before it, the ACCC considers that
the Acquisition is unlikely to give rise to any material lessening of
competition. In particular:
a. post-Acquisition, Telstra’s share of fibre pairs and/or
capacity on each of the Pacific Connect Cables and other
cables connected to Australia is expected to be small
b. there are alternative providers of subsea dark fibre and
capacity on subsea cables connected to Australia
c. the Acquisition is unlikely to foreclose access to the
remaining fibre pairs on the Pacific Connect Cables or to
capacity on alternative cables connected to Australia for
Telstra’s downstream rivals.
In these circumstances, the ACCC does not consider it necessary to
reach a concluded view on the likelihood of the notification
thresholds being met.
Given that material competition concerns are unlikely to arise, the
ACCC has determined that the Acquisition is not required to be
notified.
The ACCC considers that the determination is consistent with the
object of the Act and the interests of consumers in promoting
competition.

notification waiver applications and to assessing competition
effects more generally, see the ACCC’s interim guidance on
notification waivers and merger assessment guidelines.

determination_table_content.details:
Uber Technologies, Inc (Uber) proposes to acquire 100% of the

share purchase and transfer agreement (the Acquisition). Following
completion, Blacklane will become a wholly owned indirect
subsidiary of Uber.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Uber, is a US-based ride-hailing and food delivery
platform founded in 2009 that operates in over 70 countries,
including across Australia, where it launched in 2012.
Uber offers a range of products on its ride-hailing platform with
different levels of service, each operating largely on an on-demand
model. These products include its core products, Uber X, Uber X
Share, Uber XL and Uber Comfort, as well as its premium product
Uber Black.
The target, Blacklane, is a German-headquartered global luxury
chauffeur platform, founded in 2011 and which operates in over 50
countries. Blacklane’s platform connects customers with licensed
local chauffeurs offering a high level of service and manages the
end-to-end customer experience (booking, pricing, payment,
support).
Blacklane provides airport transfer, city-to-city and by-the-hour
limousine services. These services are available in Adelaide,
Brisbane, Gold Coast, Ipswich, Melbourne, Perth, and Sydney.

Overlap and relationship
between the parties
determination_table_content.details:
Uber and Blacklane (together, the Parties) both:
• supply premium passenger road transport services to
consumers via an online or application-based platform, and
• acquire services from drivers.
Uber’s current premium offering in Australia is known as ‘Uber
Black’. Information before us indicates Blacklane’s service level is
higher than that offered by Uber Black. Blacklane also has more
rigorous eligibility and training requirements for its chauffeurs than
Uber Black does for its drivers.
Uber recently launched ‘Uber Elite’, which offers a similar level of
service to that offered by Blacklane, in 3 cities in the United States. It
is possible that Uber Elite may also be launched in Australia.

and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition

regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.

the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form and feedback received from third parties.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
• Blacklane has a very limited presence in Australia.
• The Parties are not currently close competitors. Uber Black is
generally not viewed by relevant customers as substitutable with
the luxury service offered by Blacklane. If Uber Elite was
launched in Australia, the parties would compete more closely in
the geographic area(s) in which that service was made available.
• Even if luxury chauffeur services fall within a premium
passenger services market, the market share aggregation
arising from the Acquisition is estimated to be low. In relation to
any narrower market for luxury chauffeur services, due to the
limited presence of Blacklane in Australia, the loss of future
potential competition between Uber (through the possible
launch of Uber Elite) and Blacklane is not likely to be substantial.
• There are multiple alternative suppliers of premium passenger
road transport in Australia, including several with a national
presence. The competition that Uber faces, in terms of supplying
premium passenger road transport services and acquiring
services from drivers, is not significantly impacted by the
Acquisition.
• While the merged entity is likely to benefit from Uber’s
integration of Blacklane into the Uber booking platform, rival
chauffeur providers would continue to have alternative channels
to reach their customer base and are accordingly unlikely to be
foreclosed.
• Similarly, while Uber may be able to link ride hail with chauffeur
services in contracts with corporate customers, this would be
unlikely to foreclose rival chauffeur providers from competing
due to a range of factors, including the availability of alternative
routes to market for chauffeur operators.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines and interim merger process guidelines.

In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered the information and documents that were submitted with the notification form, additional information provided by the merger parties, market feedback and publicly available information.
For the reasons given below, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into effect.
Overlap between the parties

The parties both operate holiday parks in Busselton and Katherine. In both local areas, the parties overlap in the supply of short-term roofed accommodation and powered caravan and camping sites. The parties do not overlap in the Halls Gap and Grampians areas.
Competition assessment

The ACCC has considered the effects of the Acquisition by comparing the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition proceeds against the continuation of the current state of competition (being the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition does not proceed).
Relevant areas of competition
The ACCC considered the effect of the Acquisition on competition in the supply of powered caravan and camping sites in each of Katherine and Busselton.

The ACCC considered whether short-term roofed accommodation, such as cabins, hotels and motels, was substitutable for powered camping and caravan sites. The ACCC concluded that such substitutability would be weak. Powered and caravan and camping sites serve self-setup travellers bringing their own caravan, camper or tent, meaning they are unlikely to see a cabin, hotel or motel as a close substitute. In addition, short stay roofed accommodation is generally priced higher than caravan and camping sites.

The ACCC also considered whether unpowered sites were substitutable for powered sites. The ACCC considers unpowered sites would likely be weaker substitutes, as consumers may require or prefer powered sites for operating their caravans.

For the purposes of this assessment, it was not necessary for the ACCC to form a concluded view on the precise scope of the affected markets, because it does not materially alter the ACCC's competition assessment.

The ACCC also considered the effect of the Acquisition in the supply of short-term roofed accommodation, such as cabins, hotels and motels in Katherine and Busselton, but this theory of harm was not supported by the material before the ACCC.
Horizontal unilateral effects in the supply of powered camping and caravan sites
Busselton

The ACCC considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of powered sites in Busselton. The parties do not supply unpowered sites in Busselton.

In Busselton, the merged entity would continue to face competition from five providers with comparable amenities to the merged entity, four of which have a similar capacity of powered sites . Katherine
The ACCC considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of powered camping and caravan sites in Katherine.
The ACCC estimated that post acquisition, DHP would have a large proportion (an estimated 40%) of powered sites currently available in Katherine, with other suppliers generally being smaller.

The ACCC has considered how closely each of the suppliers of powered and caravan and camping sites in the Katherine local area compete, having regard to the quality and range of facilities offered, their distance from the target site, their capacity, and the price of staying at a powered and unpowered site. In reaching its decision, and based on the materials before it, the ACCC makes the following findings:

items: The Parties compete closely, both being in the Katherine local area, and having similar pricing and amenities.

The merged entity would continue to face competition from alternative suppliers of powered caravan and camping sites offering substantially similar amenities within the Katherine local area, and that have capacity for more customers.
